items.name: Maersk
clues: It moves boxes. Very big boxes, quite slowly, across very big oceans.
Factories, supermarkets and online shops that need their goods brought from the other side of the world.
A Danish sea captain and his son started it in 1904, in a small harbour town in the south of Denmark.
In June 2017 a cyberattack shut down its computers worldwide. It reinstalled 45,000 PCs and 4,000 servers in about ten days.
A white seven-pointed star on a light blue background, painted on hundreds of ships and countless containers.
A Danish family name that begins with “Mae” and ends in “rsk”.

items.name: FedEx
clues: It moves parcels overnight, mostly by plane, while you are asleep.
Businesses sending urgent documents and spare parts, and anyone who has ever paid extra for “next day”.
An American founded it in 1971. On its first big night, in April 1973, 14 small jets carried 186 packages between 25 US cities.
Every night its planes fly into one giant hub in Memphis, Tennessee, where the parcels are sorted before dawn and flown out again.
Purple and orange letters, with a white arrow hidden between the last two. In the film Cast Away, Tom Hanks plays one of its employees.
A short form of its original name, Federal Express.

items.name: DHL
clues: It promises to get your package anywhere in the world, quickly. Then it leaves a card saying you weren’t at home.
Online shoppers, companies sending urgent documents, and Formula 1 teams.
Three Americans started it in San Francisco in 1969, flying ships’ papers to Honolulu themselves so customs could start work before the ship arrived.
Today it belongs to what used to be Germany’s national post office, with its head office in Bonn.
Bright yellow vans with red letters.
Three letters: the first letters of the three founders’ surnames.

items.name: Aldi
clues: It sells food, and lots of things you didn’t know you needed, as cheaply as it possibly can.
Students, families, and people who pop in for milk and come out with a tent and a drill.
Two brothers took over their mother’s small shop in Essen after the Second World War. In 1960 they split the business in two, north and south.
Many products go on the shelf in the cardboard boxes they were delivered in, and there are far fewer brands than in an ordinary supermarket.
A big letter A on a blue background, a small car park and a weekly leaflet of special offers.
The first two letters of the family name, Albrecht, plus the first two of the German word for discount, Diskont.

items.name: Zara
clues: It sells clothes that look a lot like what was on the catwalk a few weeks ago.
Young people who want the latest look without paying designer prices.
Its first shop opened in 1975 in A Coruña, in the north-west of Spain.
It is famous for speed: a new design can go from the drawing board to its shops in a few weeks.
Simple black-and-white shops, very little advertising, and long queues for the changing rooms.
The founder wanted to call it Zorba, after a film, but a bar nearby already had that name, so he rearranged the letters.

items.name: Apple
clues: It makes expensive things that people have queued outside shops all night to buy.
Students with stickers on their laptops, designers, and people who like everyone to see their phone.
Three men started it in California in 1976. The third sold his share after twelve days, for $800.
The back of many of its phones said where they were designed and where they were assembled: two different countries. Its current boss used to run its supply chain.
A piece of fruit with a bite taken out of it.
The fruit that is said to have fallen on Isaac Newton’s head.
